pages.title: The FAST-HIPPOS window
pages.html:
FAST-HIPPOS opens in your web browser, but it runs on your own computer: nothing leaves it. Start it with the desktop shortcut. If it is already running, the shortcut opens the running window again, in a new tab in front; the old tab closes itself, so that there is always one.

The settings are on the left, in cards that follow the steps of the analysis: Images, Cell segmentation, Stimulation and calibration, Screening and Display and output. The Run card on the right checks the settings, starts the analysis, shows its progress and opens the results.

Finding your way

Everything in one tab. The bar at the top switches between the pages of FAST-HIPPOS, all in this browser tab:

  • Setup: the settings and the Run card (this page);
  • Experiment: the overview of all samples of the experiment folder;
  • Sample: the overview of one sample; the menu next to it lists the samples with their label and hits and loads another sample into the window (its images, folder, label and the settings of its single images; the analysis settings stay), or starts a ＋ New sample;
  • Image: the dashboard of one image (the menu next to it chooses the image).

Links in the overviews (an image, a cell, a sample) open the page in the window, and the browser's back button goes back. ↗ opens the page shown in a tab of its own, for instance to see two pages side by side; Ctrl + click on a link does the same. The pages themselves stay single files in the experiment folder, which open in any browser.

Hover over anything. Every setting has a hover text that explains what it does and when to change it. The same texts are collected in All settings.

The manual in the window. ? Help opens this manual in a panel on the right. The ? behind the title of a card opens the part about that card; ? or F1 opens the part about the card under the mouse. The dashboards and the overviews have the same help.

Basic and advanced settings. Each card shows the settings that a typical run needs. All others are under Advanced settings at the bottom of the card, grouped under subheadings. When advanced settings differ from the defaults, the card says so (Advanced settings · 1 changed) and they are marked, and the line at the top of the window counts all changed settings that are hidden. Show all advanced settings opens them all at once.

Greyed-out settings have no effect with the current choices; the hover text says why. For instance the stimulation frames when Baseline only is ticked, or the screening settings when screening is off.

Folding. Click the title of a card to fold it; Fold all folds all cards. FAST-HIPPOS remembers which cards are folded, and also the light or dark look (◐).

The cards

Images

The images to analyze and where the results go. Every image is a sample: it is analyzed in a run of its own, with the settings of the window, and gets its own folder, overview, hit list and .rgn files. With one image you have an experiment of one sample.

  • Experiment folder: always needed. The folder that holds one folder per sample, and the overview of all samples. Adding images without one proposes a folder FAST-HIPPOS next to the images. See A screen of several samples.
  • Add images…: time-lapse .tif files (ImageJ hyperstacks) or Leica .lif files. Every series of a .lif file is a sample of its own, with a tick box in its row: untick the series you want to leave out.
  • Add tile folder…: a folder of tiles exported from LAS X, which FAST-HIPPOS stitches by their stage positions into one image (one sample); see Back to the microscope.
  • Every image shows what was read from it: size, frames, channels, pixel size, frame interval, and whether it holds stage positions.
  • Below the images, one row per sample: its name (its folder in the experiment folder; the image name, which you can change) and an optional label, e.g. the condition, shown in the overviews. A row says has results: replaced when the experiment already holds a sample of that name. ▶ Run analysis analyzes the rows one after the other.
  • Image type: what the pixel values mean, and so how the value per cell is computed: two-component TCSPC fits (with τ₁ and τ₂), Fast FLIM, TauContrast, frequency-domain FLIM, ratio imaging, or intensity only.
  • Additional channel: optionally a channel whose intensity is measured per cell, e.g. a transfection marker. The cells can then be split into positive and negative cells.

Cell segmentation

How the cells are found, in a projection of the time-lapse:

  • Cellpose with a model: cyto3 or nuclei (Cellpose 3), cpsam (Cellpose 4, Cellpose-SAM), or a model of your own. A label shows the Cellpose version and whether the GPU is used, or what is wrong.
  • Existing label image: a segmentation made elsewhere, e.g. in Fiji, with one number per cell.
  • Threshold + watershed: a classical segmentation, without Cellpose. It uses an automatic (Otsu) threshold on the projection and the Cell diameter to split touching cells (0 = 20 px). Dim cells next to bright ones can be missed: then set Gamma before segmentation (advanced) to e.g. 0.5.

Cell diameter 0 lets Cellpose estimate it. Small objects can be removed with Minimum cell size; the advanced settings also filter on circularity and intensity, and choose which frames are projected.

Stimulation and calibration

When the stimulus and the calibration happened. Leave the frames empty and FAST-HIPPOS detects them in the average trace of all cells; or fill in the first frame with the stimulus (counting from 0). When you set only one of them, the other is still detected (the calibration after the stimulation, or the stimulation before the calibration).

  • No calibration: for experiments without a calibration, e.g. a transient response. Only the stimulation is looked for (or set), and the response lasts until the end of the movie. Without it, the decay of a transient can be taken for a calibration.
  • Baseline only: for movies without stimulation. When no stimulation is found in a movie, it is analysed as baseline only as well (the log says so, and the overview flags it).

Below the frames, the card lists the images that have settings of their own, for instance another stimulation frame.

Screening

Tick Screen for hits and add the hit criteria: a cell value, < or >, and a threshold. Several criteria can be required together (AND), or be alternatives of which one is enough (OR). The thresholds are easiest to set in the dashboard, after the analysis; see Choosing the hits. Classify cells on the additional channel splits the cells on the marker intensity.

The advanced settings hold the response window, the quality gates, the sorting of the hit list, and everything about stage positions and .rgn files.

Display and output

The colour scale of the lifetime images, the size of the dashboards, and which files are saved. The defaults suit most runs, and colours and ranges can also be changed in the dashboard.

The Run card

Checks. The top of the card checks the settings against the images, all the time. Red problems would stop the analysis and disable Run analysis: no images, frames beyond the end of the movie, a calibration before the stimulation, Cellpose not found. Orange warnings point out surprises: images without stage positions get no .rgn files, a sample already has results (it will be replaced), Cellpose will run without GPU.

▶ Run analysis analyzes the samples of the Images list, one after the other: segmentation, traces, stimulation detection, screening, dashboards; then it updates the experiment overview. If samples of the same name already have results, FAST-HIPPOS first tells you which will be replaced.

↻ Re-apply this sample redoes only the part after the segmentation and the traces (stimulation detection, screening, hit lists, .rgn files, dashboards) for the sample chosen in the top bar, with the current settings. It takes seconds instead of minutes. Use it after changing screening settings.

■ Stop stops a running analysis; the results of the previous run are then kept.

The card also lists the samples of the experiment and warns when some were analyzed with other settings than those in the window. ↻ Re-apply all samples re-applies the settings of the window to every sample, and ＋ New sample (top right, and in the sample menu of the top bar) starts the next sample with the same settings.

The log shows the progress. When the analysis is done, the buttons below it open the Overview of this sample, the Dashboard of each image, the sample folder (Open sample folder) and the Experiment overview, all in the window (as the top bar does) or in the file explorer.

Settings files

FAST-HIPPOS remembers the settings of the window (after every change, and the settings applied from a dashboard), and starts with them next time. Every run also saves its settings in the folder of the sample (fast_hippos_settings.toml). Open settings… loads such a file, Save settings… saves the current settings, and Defaults goes back to the default settings (the images and the experiment folder stay). Both keep the Cellpose environments you set, since they belong to the computer rather than to an experiment (unless the loaded file names its own). Settings files can also be used on the command line.

Quitting

Quit stops FAST-HIPPOS, and a running analysis, after asking. When you just close the browser tab, FAST-HIPPOS stops by itself after 15 minutes.

pages.title: The dashboard
pages.html:
Every image gets a dashboard: one page with the image, the traces of all cells, their values and the screening, all linked. It is a single file, dashboard.html in the image's folder inside the folder of its sample. In the FAST-HIPPOS window, Image in the top bar opens it (its menu chooses the image). It needs no internet, no server and no FAST-HIPPOS: open it in any browser, or send the experiment folder to a colleague.

The top bar

The name of the image, the number of cells and frames, the stimulation and calibration frames (auto = detected, set = from the settings, this image = set for this image only) and the number of hits. Below it: play the time-lapse, the frame, the lookup table and the lifetime range of the images, the traces (raw or smoothed), which cells are shown, and how to select (box or lasso). ↑ Overview goes to the overview of the sample, ◐ switches between light and dark.

Everything is linked

Hover over a cell in the image, a trace, a kymograph column, a point in the scatter plot or a row in the table: the cell is highlighted (yellow, or orange in the light theme) everywhere, and the Cell card shows it in detail.

Select cells by clicking; Ctrl + click adds or removes a cell. Shift + drag selects a box or a free-hand lasso in the image and the scatter plot (L switches between them), or a range of columns in the kymograph. The selection is outlined in all views. Esc clears it.

The panels

Screening

The pane at the top shows how the hits are chosen, and lets you change it: the timing, the quality gates, the classification on the additional channel, the hit criteria and the output. Every change takes effect at once in all views. This has its own page: Choosing the hits. Fold the pane with ▾ to make room.

Image

The lifetime image of the current frame: colour shows the lifetime, brightness the intensity. Outlines (below the image) shows the outlines of all cells, of the hits, or of the selection only; untick it (or press O) to see the image without any outlines.

  • Ctrl + scroll zooms, dragging pans, double-click zooms in on a cell, F (or Fit) shows the whole image; zooming out stops there. Zoom to selection (Z) zooms to the selected cells, or to the hits.
  • The percentage above the image is the current zoom; 1:1 (1) shows the image at 100 %, one image pixel per screen pixel. When zoomed in, a small frame at the top left shows where you are in the image.
  • Lifetime spatial smoothing (Ratio spatial smoothing for ratio images) averages the colours over 3 × 3 pixels (or 5 × 5, 7 × 7, or off), which makes them less noisy; the brightness stays sharp. Over time the image is smoothed as the traces are (time smoothing under Timing, while the traces show the smoothed values); the image then says so at the bottom right. Neither changes the values of the cells. For intensity images the spatial smoothing is greyed out: their colours are the intensity itself. The window sets how both start (Display and output → Advanced settings → Smoothing).
  • Cells colours the cells by a value instead, for instance their response, so that you see where the responders are. Intensity plays the intensity as a movie, or shows its projection.
  • route shows the visiting order of the hits in the .rgn files.
  • ⤢ shows the image full-screen.

Large images (longer than 1024 pixels) are shown as an overview; zooming in loads the full resolution for the visible part.

Traces

The lifetime over time. With few cells you see every trace; with many cells, the median of each group (hits in pink, other cells in grey, the selection) with bands that hold 50 % and 80 % of the cells, or a density map (View). The coloured backgrounds mark the baseline (blue), the response (orange) and the calibration (green).

Kymograph

All cells side by side, time running down, colour = lifetime. sort on orders the cells, for instance on their mean response, lowest first: the weak responders are then on the left. The pink ticks at the top mark the hits.

Distribution and Scatter

The distribution of the lifetimes in the current frame, with the hits and the selection outlined. log makes the count axis logarithmic, so that a few cells in a tail stay visible next to a high peak, for instance the low responders of a screen. The scatter plot shows any two values against each other, optionally on log axes, with the cells that are positive for the additional channel outlined. A lasso in the scatter plot (Shift + drag) selects a population, for instance all cells with a low baseline and a high response.

Cell

The cell under the mouse, or the last cell clicked: a crop that plays along with the time-lapse, its trace (in colour) against the average of all cells (grey), its baseline (dotted), and for every quality gate and criterion its value and whether it passes (✓). This is the place to see why a cell is, or is not, a hit.

Cells

All cells with all their values. Click a column header to sort. Rows shows all cells, the hits, the selection or the valid cells. Select hits selects the hits.

Exports

Button Gives
Rows → TSV the table as shown (a tab-separated text file; opens in Excel)
Selection → .rgn the stage positions of the selected cells, for LAS X
Hits → .rgn, Hits → TSV (Screening pane) the current hits
Settings → TOML (Screening pane) the screening settings, as a settings file

The dashboard remembers

Each dashboard remembers its display settings: colours, ranges, plot choices, scatter axes. After a reload, for instance when new results arrive after Apply, it also keeps the frame, zoom and selection.

Keys

Key
Space play / pause the time-lapse
Left Right previous / next frame
F fit the image
Z zoom to the selection (or the hits)
1 show the image at 100 %
O show or hide the cell outlines
L switch between box and lasso selection
Esc clear the selection
? or F1 the manual, at the part about the panel under the mouse (also: the ? behind a panel title, ? Help in the top bar)

pages.title: Choosing the hits
pages.html:
You rarely know the right threshold before you have seen the data. That is why the whole screening can be changed in the dashboard, after the analysis: you drag a threshold and see at once which cells become hits, in the image, the traces and the table. When the hits look right, you apply the settings, which also makes new .rgn files of the sample.

Hits are chosen per sample: the criteria, the sorting and the .rgn files belong to the sample of the dashboard (use Re-apply all samples in the window to give all samples the same criteria; see A screen of several samples).

A cell is a hit when it

  1. passes the quality gates (it is valid), and
  2. meets the hit criteria.

Before that, the timing decides which frames are the baseline, the response and the calibration, and so the values of every cell.

Timing

The plot shows the average trace of all cells, with the baseline (blue), the response (orange) and the calibration (green).

  • Stimulation and calibration. Drag the S and C markers, or type the frames. Frames count from 0 and mark the first frame with the stimulus. reset goes back to the frames found by the analysis. baseline only is for movies without stimulation. An empty cal means: no calibration (for experiments without one).
  • margin: frames left out before each transition, so that a stimulus halfway through a frame doesn't count as baseline.
  • response window: the frames whose average is the mean response (response_mean_diff and response_mean_abs). full uses the whole response (in the window and in settings files: an empty Response window); frames uses a number of frames, counted after S (the early response) or before C (the late response), with an optional margin.
  • time smoothing averages the traces over ± this number of frames, for noisy data (and the image, see the dashboard). rise is the fraction of the maximal response that defines the rise time (rise_time_frames).

Quality gates

Gates remove cells whose traces cannot be trusted; every hit must pass them. Each gate shows the histogram of its value over all cells, with draggable limits, and how many cells fail.

The gates are in the unit of the measured value: ns for lifetimes, ratio units for ratio imaging, intensity for intensity data. Their default values (0.5–1 ns and 0.2 ns) are meant for lifetimes; for ratio and intensity data the gates start switched off. Switch them on in the dashboard: they then start with a range that all cells pass, which you narrow on the histogram. When hardly any cells pass the gates, the log warns about it.

  • calibration − baseline: how much the cell responds to the calibration. A cell that doesn't respond to the maximal stimulus probably has no working sensor, or isn't a healthy cell.
  • |baseline − population|: how far the baseline of the cell is from that of all cells. Very different baselines often mean a segmentation error or a dead cell.

A gate can be switched off with its tick box.

Additional channel

With an additional channel (for instance a marker of transfection, or of one cell line in a mixed population), the cells are split in two classes on its intensity. Drag the threshold, or click Otsu to let the histogram decide. The class (ch+ or ch−) is shown per cell, and can be used in criteria and in the scatter plot.

Hit criteria

Each criterion is a cell value, <, > or between (↔), and a threshold. The histogram shows the value over all cells, with the passing cells in pink, and … pass counts them. Drag the black marker to change the threshold.

  • + criterion adds a criterion. Hover over a value in the list for its meaning, or see Cell values.
  • AND / OR: click the label of a criterion to switch. AND criteria are all required; of the OR criteria at least one must pass. For example AND baseline < 2.4, OR response < 0.5, OR rise time > 5 gives cells with a low baseline that either respond weakly or slowly. (The rise time is only meaningful for cells that respond: combine it with an AND criterion on the response.)
  • × removes a criterion.

In the example

The example screen looks for ADRB2 knock-out cells among wild-type cells: cells that hardly respond to isoproterenol. Wild-type cells saturate the sensor at about 3.25 ns, so the criteria are response_max_abs < 3.1 (the lifetime stays low) AND baseline_mean between 2.0 and 2.7 (a normal baseline). The gate calibration − baseline (0.5–1.2 ns) makes sure that every hit still responds to the forskolin calibration; the |baseline − population| gate is off. The knock-out cells carry a marker (the additional channel), so here you can check the result: in the scatter plot of additional_intensity (log) against the lifetime during the response, 64 of the 75 hits are marker-positive.

Hits from selection. Instead of criteria, you can also pick the hits by hand: select cells (click, lasso, table), switch Hits from to selection and click Use selection. Add selection adds more cells.

Output

  • sort hits by: the order of the hits in the lists (e.g. strongest response first); by default the cell order.
  • .rgn chunks of: the maximum number of positions per .rgn file. LAS X handles at most about 1000.
  • optimize path: order the positions so that the microscope travels a short route. Compute route computes it for the current hits; show in image draws it.
  • Hits → .rgn, Hits → TSV: save the current hits of this image. Settings → TOML: save these settings.

Apply the settings

What you change in a dashboard first only affects that dashboard. To make it count, use one of the two Apply buttons. They are only there when the dashboard was opened from the FAST-HIPPOS window (with Dashboard, the Image menu or via an overview), because FAST-HIPPOS itself does the work.

↻ Apply to all images uses these screening settings for all images of the sample (usually one). FAST-HIPPOS redoes the screening, the hit list and the .rgn files with their routes, the overview of the sample and of the experiment, and the dashboards. The segmentation and the traces are kept, so it takes seconds. A message lists the images first, and says what happens to images that have settings of their own. Other samples are not changed; to give them the same settings, use Re-apply all samples in the window.

↻ Apply to this image only keeps the settings of the window, and gives this image its own stimulation frames and response window, for instance when its stimulation was missed or started later. See Settings for single images.

After applying, the dashboard reloads with the new results, and the FAST-HIPPOS window shows the new settings, so that a later Re-apply this sample or Run analysis uses them too.

Changed your mind?

Reset (top right of the Screening pane) brings back the settings with which the dashboard was made.

pages.title: Settings for single images
pages.html:
All samples of an experiment are analyzed with the settings of the window, so that they can be compared. Sometimes one image needs different timing: its stimulation started a few frames later, its calibration was missed by the automatic detection, or its response is so slow that it needs another response window. For these cases an image can get its own settings, without changing those of the other samples. (The image belongs to a sample; a sample made with a settings file may hold several images, and then the other images of the sample keep their settings too.)

What can differ per image:
Stimulation stimulation frame, calibration frame, no calibration, baseline only, margin, and the detection threshold (only in a settings file)
Response window length, anchor (after S / before C) and margin

Everything else, in particular the quality gates and the hit criteria, stays that of the sample: a hit means the same for all images that you compare.

Give an image its own settings

  1. Open the dashboard of the image from the FAST-HIPPOS window (the Image menu in the top bar, or via an overview).
  2. In the Screening pane, correct the timing: drag S and C, or type the frames. Change the response window if needed.
  3. Click ↻ Apply to this image only.

FAST-HIPPOS shows exactly what will become the image's own settings, e.g. stimulation frame 7, calibration frame 22. After you confirm, it re-applies the sample of the image (its hit list, .rgn files and overview, and the experiment overview), and the dashboard reloads. Other samples are not changed.

Several images in a sample

A sample made with a settings file can hold several images. They keep their results, but the hit list, the .rgn files and their routes of the sample are made again, so that they include the corrected image.

Where you see them

  • Dashboard: an own settings label in the top bar (hover over it for the values), and the timing shows (this image) instead of (auto) or (set).
  • FAST-HIPPOS window: under Stimulation and calibration, a list of the images with their own settings.
  • Overviews (of the sample and of the experiment): an own settings label next to the image name, and image next to its stimulation and calibration frames.
  • Log: Own settings of this image: … for each such image.
  • Output folder: in settings_used.json and fast_hippos_settings.toml, and as a column of run_summary.tsv.

Remove them

In the FAST-HIPPOS window, click ✕ next to the image under Stimulation and calibration, and then Re-apply this sample (or Run analysis). The image then uses the settings of the window again.

How they combine with Apply to all images

Apply to all images uses the screening settings of the dashboard for all images of the sample (see Choosing the hits). From the dashboard of an image with its own settings:

  • If you changed the timing there, that timing becomes the timing of all images of the sample, this one included: its own timing is replaced.
  • Its own response window stays, unless you changed the response window there.
  • Other images with their own settings keep them. The confirmation message names them.

Re-apply all samples (Run card) keeps the own settings of every image.

Images in a new sample

Own settings belong to images by name, and are kept by the FAST-HIPPOS window for later runs (＋ New sample empties them). When you analyze images of the same names again (Position 1 …), check the list under Stimulation and calibration. The window warns about it, and the confirmation of Run analysis lists the images that will use their own settings.

pages.title: The overviews
pages.html:
There are two overviews, which work in the same way: the overview of one sample, and the overview of the whole experiment, which compares all samples (A screen of several samples). This page describes the panels that both have. Did the cells respond? Are there images with few cells, or without calibration? Where are the hits? The overview of a sample is index.html in the folder of the sample; in the FAST-HIPPOS window it is Sample in the bar at the top. The overview of the experiment is index.html in the experiment folder, and Experiment in the bar. Like the dashboards they are single files that work in any browser.

The window makes every image a sample, so the overview of a sample usually shows one image (a .lif series or a stitched tile scan is one image too). The comparison of images is made in the experiment overview. A sample with several images, for instance from fast-hippos-cli run with a settings file, has the same page with all its images.

The top bar shows the totals: samples (in the experiment overview), images, cells, valid cells, hits, and when the analysis was made and last re-applied. Run files opens the files of the sample (hit lists, .rgn files, log); Export downloads tables and .rgn files for the selected images. ? Help opens the manual next to the page; the ? behind a panel title opens the part about that panel.

Images

One row per image: a thumbnail, the number of cells and valid cells, the hits, the median baseline, the median response of all valid cells and of the hits, the calibration response, the frames and frame interval, the stimulation and calibration frames (auto = detected, set = from the settings, image = set for this image only), the fraction of cells positive for the additional channel, and the tiles and area of the scan. Hover over a column header for its exact meaning; click it to sort.

The name of an image opens its dashboard.

QC. The dot in the QC column is green when nothing stands out, orange or red when something does. Hover over it for the reason:

Flag Means
few cells fewer than 20 cells, or fewer than a quarter of the median of the images
low valid fraction less than 70 % of the cells pass the quality gates (below 40 %: red)
no stimulation / calibration none found, while most images have one
stimulation offset the stimulation is more than 3 frames from the usual frame
no calibration response the cells hardly respond to the calibration
no stage positions the hits of this image cannot be visited
no hits

These are warnings only: nothing is left out because of them.

Selecting. The panels below show the selected images, each in its own colour. Click a row to select only that image, Ctrl + click to add or remove one, Shift + click for a range; all and none at the top right.

Response over time

The median trace of the valid cells of each selected image, with a band holding the middle half of the cells. align on stimulation puts time 0 at the stimulation of every image, so that images with the stimulation at different frames line up. hits only shows the hits instead of all cells. Click a name above the plot to hide or show its curve.

Cells

One cell value compared between the images. distribution shows a histogram per image on a common axis, with the median and middle half (box), the hits as pink ticks and the threshold of the hit criterion as a dashed line. scatter plots two values against each other, with the hits ringed. log makes an axis logarithmic.

Hit positions

A map per image with its hits at their stage positions (in mm), the tiles of the scan, and the route that the microscope will follow through the .rgn files (dashed where the route visits a neighbouring image in between; images without stage positions get no map). Hover over a hit for its details; click it to open the cell in the dashboard of its image. same scale draws all maps at the same scale, to compare the scanned areas.

Hits

The hits of the selected images (unfold the panel with ▸): their rank in the sample, their .rgn file and stop number in it, their position and the value of the hit criterion. Click a row to open the cell in its dashboard.

Export

Export Gives
Hits → .rgn per image one .rgn file per selected image, in the visiting order of its sample
Hits → .rgn, selected images together one route through the hits of all selected images (only for images of one sample; not in the experiment overview)
Hits → TSV the hits of the selected images as a table
Images table → TSV the images table as shown, with the QC flags
Cells → TSV the values of the cells of the selected images

Without screening, the overview leaves out everything about hits, and is a comparison of the responses of the images.

pages.title: Back to the microscope
pages.html:
The point of a screen is to do something with the hits: photoactivate them, image them at high resolution, follow them over time. FAST-HIPPOS writes the stage positions of the hits as LAS X region files (.rgn), so that the microscope can visit them one by one.

The .rgn files

After a run with screening, the folder of the sample holds:

File
HITS_<sample>.rgn all hits of the sample
HITS_<sample>_1-1000.rgn, HITS_<sample>_1001-2000.rgn, … the hits in files of at most 1000 positions (Hits per .rgn file), each with its own short route
hits_1-1000.tsv, … the same hits as tables, in visiting order

<sample> is the name of the sample (its folder). Each file lists the positions in an order that keeps the stage travel short: the route is optimized, typically 13–18 % shorter than going from each hit to the nearest next one. The overview and the dashboards can draw these routes.

To visit the hits:

  1. In LAS X, open the Navigator.
  2. Right-click in it and choose Load regions, then choose the .rgn file. The positions appear as regions, in the visiting order of the file.
  3. Set up the experiment that should run at every position (photoactivation, high-resolution imaging, …) and start it.

Every sample has its own .rgn files, in its own folder in the experiment folder (see A screen of several samples): run the sample, visit its hits, then go on with the next sample.

With more than one .rgn file, load and run them one after another; each next route starts near where the previous one ended. The .rgn files are the same as those of the Fiji version of FAST-HIPPOS.

Need other hits than the analysis gave? The dashboard (Hits → .rgn, Selection → .rgn) and the overview (Export) save .rgn files of the current hits, or of a hand-picked selection.

Where the stage positions come from

To compute the stage position of a cell, FAST-HIPPOS needs the stage position of its image, and the pixel size. Usually these are read from the images:

  • Leica .lif files: every image has its position in the file. A tile scan in a .lif is stitched, with the position of every tile.
  • TIFFs exported from LAS X: from the MetaData folder that LAS X writes next to them. Keep it with the images. An image stitched by LAS X has one stage position, that of its centre (see Tile scans).
  • Images stitched by FAST-HIPPOS, or by Stitch tiles in Fiji: from their metadata.

The Images card shows for every image whether it has stage positions. For other images, choose a Stage positions file under Screening → Advanced settings: a text file with the X and Y stage position (in metres) of every image, in the order of the images, separated by spaces, tabs, commas or new lines (it replaces the positions in the images); or the .lif file with the positions (used only for images without positions of their own).

Images without stage positions are still analyzed and screened, but their hits get no .rgn file; the window warns about this before the run. A stage positions file is only read by Run analysis, not by Re-apply this sample.

Stage coordinates and the .rgn frame

The positions file holds the stage X and Y as LAS X stores them in the image metadata (the same as Bio-Formats shows). The positions in the .rgn files and in the tables (abs_x_m, abs_y_m, in metres) are in the frame of the LAS X Navigator, measured to the cell. By default, the .rgn X is the negative stage Y, and the .rgn Y the negative stage X, as on the Leica Stellaris where this was validated. So don't be surprised that they look swapped and negative.

Microscopes, even of the same type, can differ in this. Check it once on your microscope: load a .rgn file in the Navigator and see whether the positions land on the cells. If they don't, change the settings under Screening → Advanced settings → Stage axes in the .rgn files:

Setting Change it when the positions in the Navigator are
.rgn: swap stage X and Y rotated by 90°, or mirrored along the diagonal
.rgn: invert X mirrored left–right
.rgn: invert Y mirrored top–bottom

Re-apply this sample uses changed settings: the .rgn files are written again, without a new segmentation.

Hit positions on the nucleus

By default a hit position is the centre of the cell. With a Nuclei classifier (Cell segmentation → Advanced), trained on a few scribbles with fast-hippos-cli train-classifier, it becomes the centre of the nucleus, which is more precise for bean-shaped or irregular cells.

Tile scans

A large area is usually imaged as a tile scan. There are two ways to analyze it.

Stitched by LAS X. Export the stitched image (with its MetaData folder) and add it with Add images…, like any other image. It has one stage position, that of its centre, and FAST-HIPPOS computes the position of every cell from its distance to that centre. This is exact as long as the stitching only puts the tiles side by side at their nominal places: it must not shift or warp tiles, for instance to align overlapping tiles on their content. Check this once with a .rgn file in the Navigator, preferably with hits near the edges of the scan.

Tiles exported, stitched by FAST-HIPPOS. When the stitching does shift tiles, or to be independent of how LAS X stitches:

  1. In LAS X, export the tiles: one TIFF per tile (name_s0.tif, name_s1.tif, …), with the MetaData folder.
  2. In the Images card, click Add tile folder… and choose the folder. The stitched image is one sample.

FAST-HIPPOS reads the position of every tile, corrects the bidirectional scanning phase if Correct bidirectional scanning phase is on (once for all tiles), places each tile at its stage position, and saves the stitched image in the folder of the sample (<name>_STITCHED.tif), with the tile positions, so that it can be used again later. Tiles that overlap are not blended yet: the later tile covers the earlier one.

FAST-HIPPOS saves the tile positions it reads next to the tiles, as tile_positions.tsv, and uses that file from then on; delete it to read the positions again. If the MetaData folder is missing, choose the .lif file of the scan as Stage positions file: after the first run, the .lif file is not needed again.

pages.title: A screen of several samples
pages.html:
A screen usually goes like this: one (stitched) image per sample, every sample analyzed as soon as it has been imaged, its hits photoactivated on the microscope, and then the next sample. Afterwards, or while the screen goes on, you want to compare all samples.

That is how every analysis in FAST-HIPPOS works. Everything you analyze belongs to an experiment: a folder (the experiment folder) with one folder per sample, and an overview that compares the samples. Every image is a sample, analyzed in a run of its own, with its own hit list and .rgn files. There is no separate mode for a single image: with one image you have an experiment of one sample, and its overview is just short.

Setting it up

  1. In the Images card, choose an Experiment folder (e.g. D:\screens\ADRB2 screen). It may be empty, and you use the same folder for the whole screen. If you add images without choosing one, FAST-HIPPOS proposes a folder FAST-HIPPOS next to the images.
  2. Add the image of the first sample (or several images: each is a sample). Each sample gets a row with its name, its folder <experiment folder>\<name> (the image name; type another to change it), and a label if you like: its condition, plate or library part. The label shows in the experiment overview.
  3. ▶ Run analysis. When the run is done, the .rgn files of the sample are in its folder; see Back to the microscope.
  4. For the next sample, click ＋ New sample (top right of the window, or in the sample menu of the top bar). This keeps all settings, but empties the image list, the settings of single images and a file of hand-picked hits. Add the image of the next sample, and run.

With several images in the list, ▶ Run analysis analyzes the samples one after the other, each as a run of its own, and updates the experiment overview once at the end. A sample that already has results in the experiment folder is replaced; its old results wait in _previous_run until the new run is complete.

The bar at the top of the window shows where you are: Experiment (the overview of all samples), Sample (the overview of one sample, with a menu of all samples with their label and hits) and Image (the dashboard of one image). Choosing another sample in the menu, or clicking a sample in the experiment overview, loads it into the window: its images, folder, label and the settings of its single images; the analysis settings stay those of the window. When the images in the window were not analyzed yet, FAST-HIPPOS asks first.

Every run (and every re-apply) of a sample updates the overview of the experiment: index.html in the experiment folder. Experiment in the bar at the top shows it.

ADRB2 screen\                  ← the experiment folder
    index.html                 ← the overview of all samples
    experiment_summary.tsv     ← its images table
    plate 1\                   ← the folder of one sample (its run)
        index.html, HITS_plate 1.rgn, ...
        plate 1\dashboard.html
    plate 2\
        ...

A sample is a folder directly inside the experiment folder that holds a complete run; the samples are listed by name, with numbers in order (plate 2 before plate 10). Other folders, and folders whose name starts with _, are left out. To leave out a sample, move its folder out of the experiment folder; the overview changes at the next run, or at once with fast-hippos-cli experiment <folder> (see the command line).

Give every sample its own folder

A sample is always a folder inside the experiment folder. FAST-HIPPOS refuses to run into the experiment folder itself, and warns when results are written somewhere else: such a run is not part of the experiment.

Hits are per sample

Hit criteria, random hits, sorting and the .rgn files belong to a sample: there is no combined hit list over samples, because they are different specimens. To compare samples, use the experiment overview.

The experiment overview

It works like the overview of a sample, with the images of all samples together:

  • the top bar counts the samples, images, cells and hits, and shows when the first and the last sample were analyzed (or last re-applied);
  • the images table has a Sample column (click it for the overview of that sample) and a Label column; the hits table and the exported tables have them too;
  • the quality flags compare every image with all images of the experiment (e.g. few cells means fewer than in the other samples);
  • Samples (top right) opens the overview of every sample, and the summary table of the experiment;
  • Export saves .rgn files and tables per image, as in the overview of a sample. It has no route through the hits of several images together: the samples are different specimens.

Clicking an image opens its dashboard, as in the overview of its sample. Loading a sample into the window takes over its label; the Run card warns when the label in the window differs. Changing the screening in a dashboard and applying it re-applies that sample, and so updates the experiment overview too.

Are the samples comparable?

The results of two samples can only be compared when both were analyzed with the same settings. FAST-HIPPOS checks this in two places:

  • The experiment overview shows a warning at the top when the samples were not all analyzed with the same settings, and lists which settings differ in which samples.
  • The window warns in the Run card when samples of the experiment were analyzed with other settings than those in the window:

Not compared are the settings that do not change the results: the images and folders, the sample label, the display settings (except Time smoothing), the .rgn settings (file size, route, axes), the Cellpose environments, hand-picked hits, and the settings of single images, which are deliberate differences. When the hit criteria differ, the Cells panel draws no threshold lines.

↻ Re-apply all samples (in the Run card, next to Re-apply this sample) makes them the same: it re-applies the stimulation, screening and display settings of the window to every sample, one after the other, and then updates the experiment overview once. Each sample keeps its own segmentation and traces, its sample label, its hand-picked hits and the settings of its single images; a sample of another image type (e.g. ratio data among lifetime samples) also keeps its quality gates, hit criteria and colour range, which are in the units of its values. It takes seconds per sample. A sample that cannot be re-applied keeps its earlier results and settings; the experiment overview names it, and experiment_log.txt says why. Settings that only a new run changes (segmentation, traces, image type, …) can only be made the same by running the sample again.

Changing the hit criteria during a screen

Re-applying all samples also rewrites their .rgn files. Samples that were already photoactivated keep their cells, of course: the new hit lists then no longer match what happened on the microscope. Keep the hit criteria of a screen fixed once the first sample has been photoactivated, or note which samples were done with which criteria.

The example

The example data are an experiment of three samples: each of the three images is a sample of its own (library part 1–3), analyzed with the settings of the example. The screenshots on this page show it.

pages.title: The output folder
pages.html:
All results go into the experiment folder that you choose in the Images card. Every image is a sample, and every sample gets a folder of its own in it: one sample folder holds one run of one image, with its hit list and .rgn files. The experiment folder itself holds the overview of all samples. (A run of several images in one folder, with one combined hit list, can still be made with a settings file on the command line.)

What is in it

example_screen_1/               one sample: its folder in the experiment folder
├── index.html                 the overview of the sample
├── HITS_example_screen_1.rgn  stage positions of all its hits
├── HITS_example_screen_1_1-24.rgn  … in files of at most 1000 positions, each with its route
├── hits.tsv                   the hit list
├── hits_1-24.tsv              … per .rgn file, in visiting order
├── cell_coordinates.tsv       positions of all cells
├── run_summary.tsv            the images table of the overview
├── hit_positions.png          a map of the hits and their routes
├── run_log.txt                the log
├── fast_hippos_settings.toml  the settings of the run, to open in the window or use on the command line
├── settings_used.json         the same, as the program used them
├── run.json, hit_chunks.json  bookkeeping of the run (which files it wrote; the hits per .rgn file)
├── example_screen_1/          the image: its dashboard and tables
│   ├── dashboard.html         the dashboard
│   ├── cells.tsv              all cells: position, size, values, gates, hit or not
│   ├── lifetime_traces.tsv    the trace of every cell (and additional_traces.tsv)
│   ├── labels.tif             the segmentation: one number per cell
│   ├── weighted_lifetime.tif  the lifetime image (time-lapse)
│   ├── intensity_projection.tif
│   ├── kymograph*.tif, traces.png
│   └── tiles/                 full-resolution parts of large images, for the dashboard
└── …

The .tsv files are tab-separated tables: open them in Excel, or in Python or R. The TIFF images open in Fiji.

The experiment folder holds one such folder per sample, and adds index.html (the overview of all samples), experiment_summary.tsv (its images table, with the sample and its label) and, after Re-apply all samples, experiment_log.txt; see A screen of several samples.

Sharing

The overview and the dashboards work without FAST-HIPPOS. To share the results, copy the whole experiment folder (with the tiles folders), or for one sample just its folder.

Running again

Run analysis of a sample that already has results in the experiment folder (a sample of the same name) replaces them. FAST-HIPPOS first lists exactly what will be replaced (the image folders and the files of the run), and moves them into a subfolder _previous_run of the sample folder before it starts. When the new run is complete, _previous_run is deleted; if the run is stopped or fails, it is kept, so nothing is lost. Other files in the folder are never touched. To keep both runs, give the new sample another name.

To go back to the previous run after a stopped run: delete the partial results of the stopped run (the image folders and the files listed above), and move the contents of _previous_run back into the sample folder. Do this before the next complete run, which deletes _previous_run (the window reminds you).

Re-apply this sample keeps the segmentation and the traces of the sample, and redoes the rest with the current settings: stimulation detection, screening, hit lists, .rgn files, overview and dashboards. It takes seconds. It always processes the images of the sample as analyzed, also when the image list in the window has changed since; the window warns when they differ. Re-apply all samples does this for every sample of the experiment.

What a re-apply can change: the stimulation and calibration, the screening, the hit lists and .rgn files, and the display settings. What only a new run changes: the images, the segmentation, the traces, and a few settings that are needed while measuring (the size of the dashboards, the stage positions file).

The Apply buttons in the dashboards do a re-apply too; see Choosing the hits.

pages.title: Cell values (metrics)
pages.html:
FAST-HIPPOS measures these values for every cell. They can be used in hit criteria, for sorting the hits, as axes of the scatter plots and for colouring the cells in the dashboard. Lifetime stands for the measured quantity: the ratio for ratio imaging, the intensity for intensity-only data.

Name Meaning
baseline_mean Average lifetime of the cell before the stimulation (its baseline).
response_mean_abs Average lifetime of the cell in the response window (the value itself, not the change).
response_mean_diff Average change of the lifetime in the response window, compared with the cell's own baseline (lifetime − baseline).
response_fraction How much of its maximal response the cell keeps in the response window: response_mean_diff ÷ response_max_diff (1 = sustained, near 0 = transient).
response_max_abs Highest lifetime of the cell between the stimulation and the calibration.
response_max_diff Largest change of the lifetime after the stimulation, compared with the cell's own baseline. The usual measure of how strongly a cell responds.
response_max_diff_pop Largest lifetime after the stimulation minus the average baseline of all cells (instead of the cell's own baseline).
rise_time_frames Number of frames of the response up to and including the first frame in which the cell reaches the rise fraction (e.g. 75 %) of its maximal response (1 = already in the first frame after the stimulation). Small = fast responder. Only meaningful for cells that respond: combine it with an AND criterion on the response.
rapid_response_ratio Average response in the second half of the response period divided by that in the first half. Above 1 = still rising, below 1 = fading.
calibration_mean Average lifetime of the cell during the calibration (maximal stimulation).
calibration_diff Response to the calibration: calibration_mean − baseline_mean. Shows whether the sensor works in this cell.
baseline_dev_pop How much the baseline of the cell differs from the average baseline of all cells.
additional_intensity Intensity of the additional channel in the cell (mean over time, or the first frame).

Other values in the tables

These are in cells.tsv and in the Cells table of the dashboard (and can be shown in the scatter plot).

Name Meaning
area_px Size of the cell in pixels.
mean_intensity Mean pixel value of the cell per frame, over the frames used for the segmentation, in the units of the image (photon counts or amplitudes). The Minimum cell intensity filter uses the same value.
circularity 4π · area / perimeter²: 1 for a circle, lower for irregular shapes.
centroid_x, centroid_y Centre of the cell in the image (pixels).
pos_x_px, pos_y_px The position used for the hit: the centre of the cell, or of its nucleus with a nuclei classifier (pixels).
abs_x_m, abs_y_m That position as a stage position (metres), as written to the .rgn files: in the frame of the LAS X Navigator (see Back to the microscope).
class_additional 1 when the cell is positive for the additional channel (classification on), else 0.
valid The cell passes the quality gates.
hit The cell is a hit.

pages.title: How the analysis works
pages.html:
What FAST-HIPPOS does with your images, step by step. You don't need this to use it, but it helps to judge the results.

1. Reading and pre-processing

The images are read with their channels, frame interval, pixel size and stage positions. Optionally, the phase offset of bidirectional scanning is corrected (needed for some fast scans), and the drift of the sample is corrected by registering every frame to a reference frame (the first, the last or the previous frame): the shift of a frame is the position of the peak of its cross-correlation with the reference. For noisy images, that cross-correlation image can be blurred first (Drift: blur of the cross-correlation σ), as in the Fiji version, which used σ = 4; the default is 2 (0 = no blur). Drift: register edges aligns the edges of the cells instead of their intensity.

2. Segmentation

The cells are found once, in a projection over time of the intensity, optionally of a part of the frames or of a separate channel. The result is a label image: every cell a number. Cells can then be removed by size, circularity and intensity. The cells do not move with time: the same outlines are used in every frame.

3. Traces

For every cell and every frame, FAST-HIPPOS computes one value from all pixels in the cell:

Image type Value of a cell
Fitted TCSPC (two components) the amplitudes A₁ and A₂ of all pixels are pooled: τ = Σ(A₁τ₁ + A₂τ₂) / Σ(A₁ + A₂)
Fast FLIM, TauContrast, frequency-domain FLIM the intensity-weighted mean lifetime
Ratio imaging ΣC₁ / ΣC₂
Intensity only the mean intensity

The mean intensity of the additional channel, if any, is measured too.

4. Stimulation and calibration

If the frames are not set, they are detected in the average trace of all cells: a stimulation or calibration shows up as a sudden step, a peak in the second derivative of the trace. When one frame is set, the other is detected (the strongest step after the stimulation, or before the calibration); with No calibration only the stimulation is looked for. A peak counts when it stands out from the noise of the trace by the detection threshold (5 × the noise σ by default; lower is more sensitive). The noise is estimated robustly, so that a large calibration step does not hide a smaller stimulation.

The frames then divide every trace into the baseline (before the stimulation), the response (between the stimulation and the calibration) and the calibration, leaving out a margin of one frame before each transition.

5. Cell values

From these parts, every cell gets a set of values, such as its baseline, its mean and maximal response, its rise time and its calibration response. See Cell values.

6. Screening

  1. Quality gates keep the cells whose traces can be trusted: they respond to the calibration (calibration − baseline within a range), and their baseline is close to that of all cells. These are the valid cells.
  2. Classification (optional) splits the cells on the intensity of the additional channel (on a log scale), by Otsu's method or a threshold you set.
  3. Hit criteria: a valid cell is a hit when it passes all AND criteria, and at least one of the OR criteria (if there are any). Alternatively the hits are picked by hand.

The dashboard recomputes all of this in the browser, with the same results as the analysis.

7. Hit positions and routes

Every sample has its own hit list: the hits are chosen, sorted and written to .rgn files per sample, never over samples. The stage position of a hit is the stage position of its image plus the offset of the cell in the image (its centre, or the centre of its nucleus with a nuclei classifier). The hits are split into .rgn files of at most 1000 positions, and the order within each file is optimized to make the route of the stage short: a nearest-neighbour route, improved by 2-opt and Or-opt moves, typically 13–18 % shorter than nearest neighbour alone.

Speed and large images

On a stitched 1.9 GB data set (4089 × 2556 px, 30 frames, 3 channels, 10 239 cells), on a computer with a Quadro RTX 3000 GPU (6 GB):

Step Time
Cellpose on the GPU 1 min (cyto3, automatic diameter) to 2 min (cpsam)
everything else (measurement, screening, routes, dashboard with tiles) about 2 min
re-applying the screening 15–30 s

Images larger than 1024 px are shown in the dashboard as an overview, while full-resolution tiles are loaded for the visible area when zooming in, so that the dashboard stays responsive.

Compared with the Fiji version

The Python version follows the workflow of the Fiji macro v0.9.5, with these differences:

  • TCSPC cell lifetimes pool the fitted amplitudes of all pixels; the Fiji version averages the pixel lifetimes, weighted by intensity. The values differ slightly, most for dim cells, so thresholds do not transfer exactly.
  • Frames count from 0 and denote the first frame with the stimulus: Fiji frames s,c become stimulation frame s + 1 and calibration frame c + 1.
  • The stimulation detection uses a robust noise estimate.
  • The Labkit step that puts the hit positions on the nuclei is replaced by a pixel classifier.
  • Tiles are stitched by their stage positions, without Fiji.

pages.title: Questions and problems
pages.html:
Starting

Nothing happens when I double-click the shortcut

FAST-HIPPOS may still be starting (the first start after an installation or update takes longer). If it is already running, the shortcut opens its window in the browser again. Otherwise open PowerShell in the FAST-HIPPOS folder and run uv run fast-hippos-cli gui: the console then shows what goes wrong.

The window says Cellpose is not available

FAST-HIPPOS looks for Cellpose in its own environment and in the environments set under Cell segmentation → Advanced settings. Set the python.exe of an environment with the Cellpose version that the model needs: Cellpose 3 for cyto3 and nuclei, Cellpose 4 for cpsam. See Installation.

Cellpose runs on the CPU, not on the GPU

The Cellpose environment needs PyTorch with CUDA support. Use GPU must also be on (Cell segmentation → Advanced settings). The label under the Cellpose model shows what was found.

The analysis

My experiment has no calibration

Tick No calibration (Stimulation and calibration). Only the stimulation is then looked for, and the response lasts until the end of the movie; the calibration gate is not used.

The stimulation or the calibration was not found, or found at the wrong frame

Open the dashboard of the image, drag S and C to the right frames, and click Apply to all images (the settings of the sample) or Apply to this image only. See Settings for single images. If detection fails often, lower the Detection threshold (Stimulation and calibration → Advanced settings), or set the frames in the window.

Too many or too few cells

Check the outlines in the dashboard. With Cellpose, set the Cell diameter (in pixels) instead of 0, or try another model. Minimum cell size removes debris; the advanced settings also filter on circularity and intensity.

Many cells are not valid, or there are no hits at all

The quality gates remove them (the log warns when hardly any cells pass). Look at the histograms of the gates in the dashboard: is the calibration response in the range of calibration − baseline? The gates are in the unit of the measured value; the default range (0.5–1 ns) suits the usual lifetime sensors. For ratio and intensity data the gates start off; set them from their histograms. Without hit criteria no cell is a hit.

No .rgn files were written

The images have no stage positions (the window warns about this). See where the stage positions come from.

The positions of the .rgn file don't land on the cells in the LAS X Navigator

Microscopes differ in how their stage axes relate to the Navigator. Change .rgn: swap stage X and Y, .rgn: invert X or .rgn: invert Y (Screening → Advanced settings) and click Re-apply all samples; see stage coordinates and the .rgn frame.

I changed the criteria in the dashboard, but the .rgn files did not change

Changes in a dashboard only affect that page until you click Apply to all images (or Apply to this image only), or save the hits with Hits → .rgn. The Apply buttons only appear in dashboards opened from the FAST-HIPPOS window.

Can I analyze images with different protocols?

Yes. Every image is a sample of its own. Leave the stimulation frames on automatic, or give single images their own settings. The hit criteria are those of the window, for every sample; to compare samples they should be the same (see Are the samples comparable?).

Results

I only have one image. Do I need an experiment?

You choose an experiment folder (it may be empty, and the window proposes one next to your image), and the image is a sample in it. Everything works as for a screen, and the experiment overview is just short. See Your first analysis.

Where are my results?

In the folder of the sample, inside the experiment folder you chose; see the output folder. Open sample folder in the Run card opens it.

I ran the analysis again, and my previous results are gone

A new run of a sample of the same name replaces its previous results, after asking. Give the new sample another name (its row in the Images card) to keep both. If a run did not finish, the previous results are still in _previous_run in the folder of the sample.

Can someone without FAST-HIPPOS look at the results?

Yes: send the experiment folder (or the folder of one sample). The overviews (index.html) and the dashboards open in any browser.

Still stuck?

Report it on GitHub, with the log (run_log.txt in the folder of the sample) and the settings file.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.html:
Additional channel
An extra channel whose intensity is measured per cell, e.g. a transfection marker. Cells can be classified as positive or negative on it.
Baseline
The part of a trace before the stimulation.
Calibration
A maximal stimulus at the end of the experiment, which shows how far the sensor can go in each cell. Used by the quality gates.
Criterion
A condition on a cell value, such as response_mean_diff < 0.6. AND criteria must all pass; of the OR criteria one is enough.
Dashboard
The interactive page of one image (dashboard.html).
Experiment folder
The folder that holds one folder per sample, and the overview of all samples. Every analysis in the window goes into an experiment folder, also with one image.
Hit
A valid cell that meets the hit criteria (or that you picked by hand).
Kymograph
An image with one column per cell and one row per frame: all traces at once.
Lifetime
The fluorescence lifetime of the sensor in a cell, in ns. For ratio and intensity data, read ratio or intensity.
Output folder
The folder with the results of one run: in the window, the folder of a sample. (Its name in settings files is input.output.)
Overview
A page that compares images (index.html): of one sample, in its folder, or of the whole experiment, in the experiment folder.
Sample
One specimen: every image is a sample, analyzed in a run of its own, with its own hit list and .rgn files, in its own folder inside the experiment folder. It can carry a label, e.g. its condition.
Quality gate
A condition that every hit must meet, to keep out cells whose traces cannot be trusted.
Re-apply
Redo the screening of a sample (or of all samples) with other settings, without segmenting and measuring again.
Response
The part of a trace between the stimulation and the calibration. The response window is the part of it whose average is the mean response.
.rgn file
A LAS X region file with stage positions, which the microscope can visit.
Run
One analysis of a sample with one set of settings, in one folder. (From a settings file, a run can also hold several images, with one combined hit list.)
Stimulation
The stimulus whose effect is measured, e.g. adding an agonist. Its frame is the first frame with the stimulus.
Trace
The lifetime of one cell over time.
Valid cell
A cell that passes the quality gates.
